title: Electrical Probing of Dark Excitons through Microwave Permittivity
authors: Alex Stram, Zhida Liu, Ziheng Zhang, Yangchen He, Xuejian Ma, Kyoung Pyo Lee, Lisa Frammolino, Fuxiang Chen, Robert J. Boyd, Sirapas Tangton, Anand Swain, Kan Yao, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Yuebing Zheng, Chih-Kang Shih, Daniel Rhodes, Li Yang, Xiaoqin Li, Keji Lai
abstract: Excitons in atomically thin semiconductors are almost always probed through their optical signatures, because the short lifetimes of these transient quasiparticles are generally assumed to preclude electrical detection. Here we show that photoexcited excitons in monolayer tungsten disulfide produce a large, optically tunable permittivity at gigahertz frequencies, and that the effect provides a contact-free electrical route to imaging dark excitons at the nanoscale. Using laser-illuminated microwave impedance microscopy, we find that high-purity encapsulated flakes exhibit a purely dielectric response resonant with the exciton spectrum, whereas defect-rich samples are governed by conventional photoconductivity. Spatial mapping of diffusion and sublinear power dependence identify long-lived dark excitons as the dominant contributors, and first-principles modelling of exciton polarizability reproduces the measured susceptibility. Our results establish excitons as optically tunable dielectric elements and introduce microwave microscopy as a direct electrical probe of dark-exciton transport with sub-100 nm resolution.
summary: This research introduces microwave impedance microscopy (iMIM) as a breakthrough, contact-free electrical technique to image dark excitons in 2D semiconductors like WS2. By measuring the material's complex permittivity, the authors successfully separated the purely dielectric exciton response from background conductivity. This establishes excitons as tunable dielectric elements and opens a new pathway for nanoscale quantum material characterization.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a contact-free electrical method to probe dark excitons in atomically thin semiconductors, which are typically only visible via optical spectroscopy.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated that photoexcited excitons contribute a measurable, purely dielectric permittivity at microwave frequencies, allowing for nanoscale imaging of dark exciton transport.
method: The experiment utilizes laser-illuminated microwave impedance microscopy (iMIM) to measure the complex permittivity, which is complemented by first-principles DFT and GW-BSE calculations to model the exciton polarizability.
model_or_system: The system is monolayer tungsten disulfide (WS2) and other 2D semiconductors. The theoretical framework involves modeling the exciton polarizability using an effective Keldysh electron-hole Hamiltonian and relating it to the macroscopic dielectric response via Clausius-Mossotti-like relations.
key_observables: The imaginary part of the tip admittance ($	ext{iMIM-Im}$) shows resonant peaks matching exciton spectra, while the real part ($	ext{iMIM-Re}$) remaining zero confirms a purely dielectric response, distinguishing it from photoconductivity.
important_parameters: The measurements are performed at gigahertz frequencies, with spatial resolution achieving sub-100 nm, and the response is tunable by laser power and temperature.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include the negligible out-of-plane polarizability compared to the in-plane component, and the use of the Clausius-Mossotti relation to link microscopic polarizability to macroscopic permittivity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the iMIM setup, the dependence of the effective dielectric constant on photon energy, and comparative maps showing the distinct purely dielectric response (high-purity) versus the conductive response (defect-rich) in the iMIM spectra.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the limitations of optical probing, then introducing the iMIM technique to measure the dielectric response, demonstrating the distinction between exciton-induced permittivity and conventional photoconductivity, and finally validating the findings through theoretical modeling of exciton polarizability.
why_interesting: This work bridges solid-state physics (exciton dynamics) with microwave engineering, providing a novel, non-optical diagnostic tool for quantum materials that is highly relevant to condensed matter theory.
